text: Lesson one covered why GPUs are fast at the math behind deep learning. Speed doesn't help if the job never starts in the first place. This lesson is about the constraint that actually fails training jobs most often in practice — not raw compute, but GPU memory, and what has to fit inside it.

During training, a GPU has to hold several things in its own on-board memory at the same time. The model's weights, obviously. Gradients — one value per parameter, computed during backprop. Optimizer state, which is bookkeeping the optimizer keeps per parameter — Adam, the most common choice, keeps both momentum and variance, and this is often the single largest memory consumer. And activations, the intermediate output of every layer, kept around so backprop can use them. None of this is optional, and none of it spills cleanly to regular system memory.

Work the math for a seven billion parameter model trained in FP16. Weights land around fourteen gigabytes. Gradients, another fourteen. Adam's optimizer state, commonly kept in FP32 for stability, adds roughly fifty-six gigabytes. Add activation memory on top, and full fine-tuning can need eighty to a hundred gigabytes or more — more than a single eighty-gigabyte A100 or H100 has, before you've even increased batch size.

That math is exactly why techniques like LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights instead of the full model, and eight-bit or four-bit quantization, and gradient checkpointing, which recomputes activations instead of storing all of them, and multi-GPU memory partitioning through DeepSpeed ZeRO or Fully Sharded Data Parallel all exist. Every one of them responds directly to the memory wall. That's also why 'CUDA out of memory' is the error you'll see constantly in this field.

It's worth separating two things that both get called GPU memory. Capacity is the total VRAM on the card, deciding whether your working set fits at all. Bandwidth is how fast data moves between that memory and the compute cores — datacenter GPUs use High Bandwidth Memory, with the A100 around two terabytes per second, specifically because feeding thousands of parallel cores fast enough is its own separate engineering problem.

A job can be capacity-bound, where it won't even load, or bandwidth-bound, where it loads but cores sit idle waiting on data — and the fix for each is completely different. Next lesson takes this memory math and maps it onto the real instance families you'll actually provision: Azure's NC, ND, and NV series, and AWS's P and G series.
